title: MCDM Applications for Sustainability Assessment in Textile and Apparel Supply Chains: A Systematic Review of Methods, Contexts, and Criteria
content: Sustainability in the textile supply chain involves complex trade-offs across economic, environmental and social aspects, driven by the variability in materials, manufacturing processes and technologies, industrial management, geographical locations, working conditions, logistics, and product use. While multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods have been increasingly applied to navigate these trade-offs, existing reviews have narrowly focused on bibliometric trends, offering limited insight into the contextual application and sustainability criteria used in these assessments. This study addresses this gap through a systematic literature review by analysing 96 studies that investigate the application of MCDM methods in sustainability management across the textile supply chain, with specific attention to methodological rigor and contextual relevance. The review identifies two key research dimensions: (1) the MCDM methods employed and their application contexts in respective scope of studies, and (2) the applied and prioritized criteria for sustainability management in textile industries. Results show that the identification of influential factors for sustainability implementation is the most common scope of study, with DEMATEL being the dominant MCDM tool and identifying government policies as the most influential factor. This is followed by sustainable supplier selection, with frequent use of hybrid AHP-TOPSIS methods, often in fuzzy settings, and a predominant focus on economic criteria, particularly cost and financial flexibility. The majority of corporate sustainability assessments rely on quantitative environmental data derived from corporate reports, and public data and use single-method MCDM models without explicit weighting schemes. Product-level assessments commonly employ distance-based MCDM methods to support the interpretation of Life Cycle Assessment results or to expand the sustainability perspective by incorporating economic and social dimensions. This review advances the understanding of how MCDM methods support sustainability decision-making in different contexts and settings of textile supply chain and highlights key criteria shaping such evaluations.
